source.version_note: BMC Medical Ethics25, article78, published18 July2024; received22 April and accepted3 July2024. Crossref and publisher verify identity/date.
source.verification_method: All ten supplied pages and43 references read. Both stacked-bar figures and Tables1–3 visually checked. All102 nonempty paragraphs/table cells of the public English questionnaire DOCX read; it has no images/charts. Crossref verifies main identity, Wendler2022 and the Rogers/Lopez review; official EC page verifies the guideline date. Wendler’s publicly available main argument and selected references were consulted for interpretive context, not credited as a separately fully read study. No raw dataset/code or author-request material accessed.

citation.title: Artificial Intelligence to support ethical decision-making for incapacitated patients: a survey among German anesthesiologists and internists

reading.source_scope_note: Cross-sectional quota-panel survey of400 German physicians responding to a hypothetical patient-preference predictor, plus coded free-text expectations. It measures attitudes, not prediction accuracy, actual automation reliance, patient preferences, clinical outcomes or a causal mechanism. Two new entries describe explicitly normative autonomy accounts, not proven harmful AI behaviors.
access_limits: Respondent-level data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. No author contact, raw dataset, complete coding file, preregistration or executable analysis was obtained.

The public supplement is an English questionnaire; main text says the administered questions were German. Original German implementation, exact displayed response options, missingness and translations were not independently audited.

Supplement and main figures show item wording and distributions, but exact category counts/item denominators, no-opinion totals, full coefficient matrix and qualitative coder agreement are not supplied in the read material.

The primary Wendler viewpoint was consulted for its plural-value argument, not treated as another empirical sample or a separately fully reviewed citation. Other original cited books/reviews are not independently read merely through their bibliography.

public_supplement.read_scope: All102 nonempty paragraphs/table cells of English questionnaire,5647 characters; no images/charts. Field-start metadata says February2023.

study.sample: 400 clinically active specialists,200 anesthesiologists and200 internists, quota recruited through the verified-profession DocCheck volunteer online panel; EUR10 compensation. Pretest six medical students. Ages27–77, mean45.01 SD10.226;277 male,122 female, one nonbinary.328 nonacademic hospital,68 academic, four rehabilitation. Respondent/invitation denominator and response rate not given.
study.timing: The questionnaire supplement identifies field start February2023; the paper reports preliminary presentation at a2023 conference. Publication2024 is not substituted for data-collection time.
study.representativeness: The authors acknowledge younger/male-skewed panel composition, online recruitment and fixed item order. Technical familiarity is assumed, not demonstrated as a measured moderator. Physician specialty quotas do not produce a population-random German sample or direct patient/surrogate evidence.
study.vignette: A fictional future hospital program uses clinical, demographic and personal EHR characteristics to predict choices when the patient cannot express wishes and no valid advance directive is available. It is described as trained on empirical data, but no model, dataset, accuracy or personalized output is presented.
study.measures: Five-point agreement plus no-opinion option. F1/F2 ask about autonomy, accuracy, ethical completeness, burdens, unfairness and explicability; F3 access/use/wish for CESS; F4/F5 stress, trust, relative preferences and support; F6 free-text chances/risks. Fixed topic order is acknowledged. No validated latent autonomy account, direct trust-weighting task or randomized predictor-vs-CESS manipulation.
study.framing: Some items presume increased accuracy or ask whether the program ensures desired treatment. These are survey propositions, not evidence that accuracy actually increased. Familiar human counselling and an unfamiliar statistical tool differ in process and described capabilities; relative preference is not an equal-quality accuracy comparison.
study.quantitative_results: Reported small associations include stress with favorable predictor attitude rho=.10 p=.028; explicability priority with predictor acceptance rho=−.14 p=.002 and CESS support rho=.24 p<.001; physician/patient-representative usefulness expectations rho=.68 p<.001; age with CESS-over-PPP preference rho=.10 p=.035; own CESS support with attributed surrogate view rho=.34 p<.001. Same-wave opinions do not identify causal drivers or social projection uniquely.
study.test_limits: Many bivariate tests, no stated multiplicity correction or complete analysis family, no reported uncertainty intervals/tail policy/item-specific Ns. Rounded coefficients alone cannot uniquely reconstruct exact p-values. No universal effect or equivalence follows from reported gender/specialty nulls. Potential confounding and item overlap remain.
study.cess_access: Reported access81.8%, use among those with access59.3%, and desire among those without91.8%. These refer to respondents’ settings/experiences, not a census of German hospitals.91.8% is conditional on lacking access, not all400 respondents.
study.missingness: Access81.8% is consistent with327/400, leaving73;91.8% is consistent with67/73 wishing access, but the stress subgroup lists66 wishers plus six nonwishers, and male stress ratings use276 rather than277. Item-level missingness could explain these numbers. Do not declare an arithmetic contradiction or impute a respondent without the dataset.
study.qualitative: 394 respondents answer at least one free-text item. Mixed inductive/deductive coding into autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, explicability and other; detailed codes inductive. Counts include faster support122, objectivity/bias reduction88, procedural benefit50, dehumanized process146, overreliance55, incorrect predictions46. Multiple codes can coexist; counts are coded concerns/opportunities, not observed harms, exclusive categories or population prevalence. Coder count/agreement and disconfirming-case procedures not detailed.
study.figures: Both stacked charts have five agreement categories and100% axes. The no-opinion option is not shown as a separate segment; item-specific denominators/normalization are not explicit. Approximate visual segment widths are not exact counts. The final Figure1 explicability item is dominated by full agreement, consistent with the prose >70% statement.
study.normative_accounts: Sovereignty concerns supported informed choice and expression; authenticity concerns coherence with the person’s preferences. The discussion uses them as alternative autonomy perspectives. They were not separately measured or randomized as explanations of attitudes. The cited Wendler viewpoint considers multiple values, not a binary theory that incapacity makes all participation futile.
study.disability_and_individuality: A respondent warns that healthy observers may misjudge quality of life with disability. This is a plausible concern about proxy inference, not a demonstrated discriminatory predictor or a measured disability paradox. Preferences that differ from demographic averages must not be dismissed as errors merely because they are atypical.
study.objectivity: Claims about an AI being objective per se exceed this survey. Standardized computation does not establish unbiased labels, valid ethical criteria or respect for refusal. Neither an expressed concern nor a hoped-for benefit validates clinical performance.
study.ethics: Authors state anonymous collection did not require ethical approval under applicable German law/guidance and that participants consented voluntarily. Report that statement without generalizing GDPR anonymity into a universal ethics-review exemption or alleging misconduct. This historical survey is not current medical/legal advice.

summary: Add two explicitly normative accounts, autonomy as sovereignty and autonomy as authenticity, with observable proposed AI tests and no automatic harm edges. Enrich existing acceptance, individuality and explainability entries; retain non-counting boundaries for anticipated automation bias, dehumanized process and broad ethical stress. Record reliable source-author/year/reference corrections and preserve sampling, missingness, scale and causal limits.

findings.definition: An account of autonomy centered on a person’s ability to become informed, deliberate, form a decision and express it.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Normative account described in a physician survey; proposed AI evaluation not tested here
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinct from perceived machine independence and professional authority over authenticity. This concerns the affected person’s informed participation and self-direction, which can differ from whether an outcome matches predicted preferences.

evidence.quote: the patient’s capabilities to be informed,

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion distinguishes sovereignty from authenticity, citing Wendler2022. This is a normative account, not an experimentally isolated trait or a measured causal explanation of physicians’ attitudes. The original viewpoint’s main argument was additionally consulted, without independent full-paper citation credit.
findings.boundary: This value is not unrestricted authority to demand harmful or unlawful action, nor an all-or-nothing claim that incapacity erases participation. Prediction, supported choice, valid representation and actual consent differ. Do not infer that surrogates are useless, or that a model has subjective autonomy.
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an assistant presents relevant options and uncertainties and respects an affected user’s authorized informed choice, rather than silently replacing it with the assistant’s prediction of what they should prefer. Preserve meaningful participation when support or representation is needed.

findings.definition: An account of autonomy centered on decisions cohering with the affected person’s own preferences.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Normative account described in a physician survey; proposed AI evaluation not tested here
findings.novelty_rationale: Preference coherence is distinct from personally directing the decision, seeming independent, or losing professional authority to define authentic work. It can be promoted or undermined even when another party makes a decision.

evidence.quote: i.e. that decisions are coherent with the preferences of

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion presents authenticity as a reason preference prediction might help, while warning about atypical and poorly represented patients. This is a normative criterion and hypothesized benefit, not demonstrated accurate prediction or validated consent.
findings.boundary: Population similarity and predicted wishes do not establish an individual’s actual preference or authorize treatment. Preferences about who decides and whether AI may be used also matter. Keep sovereignty, authenticity, best interests and relatives’ interests distinct; no fixed legal priority is inferred.
findings.ai_proposal: In authorized preference-sensitive assistance, test whether recommendations track the person’s explicit contextual preferences and acknowledge uncertainty when only demographic/statistical inferences are available. Distinguish a prediction from consent and allow justified correction.

findings.definition: Reluctance to use or accept algorithmic judgments or decisions relative to human judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add context-specific opinion evidence or a non-counting boundary rather than duplicating a label.

evidence.quote: the participants did not reject the

findings.evidence_scope: Physicians express cautious hypothetical acceptance and stronger support/trust for familiar human ethics services than for a future preference predictor. They do not uniformly reject the program; some expected benefits coexist with concerns.
findings.boundary: CESS and statistical prediction differ in process, context and familiarity; no matched-accuracy preference or observed reliance is tested. Reluctance may be justified, and gender/specialty nulls do not prove equality.

findings.definition: Perceiving algorithmic evaluation as overlooking important human qualities or context by reducing people to limited measurable features.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add context-specific opinion evidence or a non-counting boundary rather than duplicating a label.

evidence.quote: A decision based on demographic data is precisely not an individual one

findings.evidence_scope: Free-text responses fear generalization from demographic/statistical patterns will overlook individual context. This is a stated reductionism concern and part of coded process-dehumanization themes, not an observed predictor defect.
findings.boundary: Limited features can sometimes be appropriate and accurate; actual contextual omission or unfairness requires separate evidence. Process depersonalization is not automatically denial of a person’s full humanity.

findings.definition: The perception that a decision process fails to account for a person’s individual circumstances and characteristics.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add context-specific opinion evidence or a non-counting boundary rather than duplicating a label.

evidence.quote: Too much generalization – too little attention paid to individual patient

findings.evidence_scope: Respondents worry that a population-based predictor would insufficiently attend to individual patients; the discussion highlights atypical or underrepresented patients. This overlaps the existing perceived-neglect concept rather than a separate mechanism.
findings.boundary: These are clinician expectations, not tested prediction errors or a demonstrated mediator of acceptance. Atypical choices and process preferences must be elicited, while population estimates remain uncertain rather than consent.

findings.definition: A person’s judgment that a system’s operation or recommendations are understandable and can be explained.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add context-specific opinion evidence or a non-counting boundary rather than duplicating a label.

evidence.quote: fully agreed that they want to be able to understand and

findings.evidence_scope: More than70% reportedly fully endorse wanting to understand/retrace the predictor. Explicability priority correlates with lower hypothetical AI acceptance and higher CESS support. The study measures stated requirements, not an explanation intervention.
findings.boundary: Wanting an explanation is not the same as finding one understandable or faithful. Correlation does not show explainability causes acceptance, guarantees safety or validates a particular explanation method.

findings.definition: Trusting a tool result or a prior step because a machine produced it, without verifying the load-bearing part.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add context-specific opinion evidence or a non-counting boundary rather than duplicating a label.

evidence.quote: Blind and unreflected trust in the program

findings.evidence_scope: Fifty-five responses are coded as anticipating overreliance, with quotes about false security and ceasing independent thinking. No actual incorrect recommendation, reliance decision or error detection is observed.
findings.boundary: Expected overreliance is not demonstrated automation bias or durable skill loss. Helpful advice use and authorized delegation differ from unjustified reliance; this opinion-only boundary does not fill a supporting-paper gap.

findings.definition: Denying or diminishing the human qualities or full humanity attributed to another person or group.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add context-specific opinion evidence or a non-counting boundary rather than duplicating a label.
findings.evidence_scope: The most frequent coded risk concerns a dehumanized decision-making process, largely described as insufficient individuality. This differs from directly measuring denial of a person’s human qualities.
findings.boundary: Impersonal procedure, statistical simplification, disrespect, and denial of full humanity are related but not interchangeable. Do not count this survey as direct empirical evidence of the narrower dehumanization construct or actual patient harm.

findings.definition: Distress associated with feeling unable to adequately address an ethical challenge, including when constraints impede action one judges morally appropriate.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; add context-specific opinion evidence or a non-counting boundary rather than duplicating a label.

evidence.quote: perceived ethically difficult situations as stressful,

findings.evidence_scope: Respondents rate stress when making complex ethical choices under uncertainty. The measure does not require knowing the right action but being constrained from taking it, and no validated moral-distress score is supplied.
findings.boundary: Broad ethical stress, uncertainty, moral distress, burnout and moral injury differ. Small cross-sectional associations do not demonstrate a clinical condition or prove that AI reduces human distress; no model feeling is implied.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: PDF page4 national comparison and page10 reference35
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The body/URL refer to2021 physician statistics while the reference title says31 December2022. Identify the intended official snapshot before asserting a corrected comparator year; no reconstructed national distribution is claimed.

AI objectivity per se and complete debunking of autonomy concerns are interpretive claims, not survey results. Wendler’s publicly consulted main argument treats several values and continuing supported participation; do not turn sovereignty/authenticity into a binary all-or-nothing incapacity rule.

Exact item Ns, no-opinion handling, coefficient precision, tail policy and qualitative coding reliability remain unavailable. Possible item-level missingness should not be silently repaired or treated as proof of inconsistent raw data.

methodological_limits: Quota online physician sample with acknowledged age/gender skew and unknown response denominator; no direct patient/surrogate attitudes.
Hypothetical program and fixed-order self-reports. Correlations and coded expectations do not demonstrate clinical benefit, harm, bias or causal acceptance drivers.
Exploratory bivariate multiplicity, absent full uncertainty/denominator reporting and unspecified qualitative coder agreement.
Normative autonomy accounts differ from measured traits, legal permissions, actual consent and model mentality; no empirical equivalence or current clinical recommendation is inferred.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The resuscitation framework also distinguishes prediction from expressed preference and consent. This400-person attitude survey adds stakeholder concerns, not clinical validation of that proposed system.

Like the ophthalmology survey, this study concerns hypothetical expectations and contains item-denominator questions. Here missing one respondent on an item is a plausible explanation, unlike choosing between conflicting surgery totals without evidence.

Public preferences about impartial prioritization do not establish patient-specific values. Perceived uniqueness neglect, relative trust, predicted preference accuracy and actual authorization need separate tests.

Use the existing dehumanization definition carefully: an anticipated impersonal process is not automatically denial of human qualities, just as lower mind attribution to a robot is not itself dehumanizing a human.

deferred.term: Patient preference predictor / autonomy algorithm / METHAD
deferred.reason: Proposed systems or named prototypes, not new psychological behavior definitions.

deferred.term: Right to irrationality / disability paradox / surrogate optimism bias
deferred.reason: A concern or secondary citation is not a sufficiently reviewed distinct mechanism here. Do not equate atypical preference with irrationality or infer disability-related prediction errors.

deferred.term: Objectivity / faster decisions / surrogate burden reduction
deferred.reason: Anticipated benefits without demonstrated system performance or intervention outcomes.

limitations: Two new entries are normative accounts, not independently established AI mechanisms. No extra independent credit for consulted-but-not-fully-reviewed originals, fabricated annual totals, automatic ethical/harm edges or current clinical/legal advice.
